statement: In studies published from 2000 to 2011 in Australia, the UK, Ireland, North America and eight other European countries, mostly surveys in which health professionals reported their own attitudes, many professionals described negative attitudes towards patients with alcohol or drug problems, or regarded them less well than patients with other conditions, more often outside specialist drug and alcohol services, while several studies found moderate, neutral or positive attitudes; whether such attitudes make the care these patients receive worse was examined in only a few studies, whose results point different ways. A systematic review of 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples; 12 from Australia, 7 from the UK and 5 from the US; 20 quantitative, mostly questionnaires at one time point, five interview or focus-group studies, two implicit association tests and two using observation) gave no count or pooled estimate of how common negative attitudes were. Among its examples: among 866 professionals in eight European countries, regard was lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems compared with patients with depression or diabetes, and lowest among doctors outside specialist drug and alcohol services; in a vignette study, professionals held more stigmatizing views of active substance use disorder than of other mental illness; and at least six study summaries in the review's table describe attitudes as moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive (editors' count). More contact, experience, training and support went with more positive attitudes, in data collected at one time. On consequences for care: clients of residential rehabilitation services in Sydney who perceived more discrimination by staff were less likely to complete treatment (a mixed-methods study of 92 clients, attributed in the review's text to the wrong paper by the same team); two qualitative studies suggested that clinicians may impose their beliefs on patients, and described district nurses making shorter, task-focused visits; among 2,864 patients with HIV, 17.1% of them currently injecting drugs, physicians' negative attitudes were not associated with patients' reports of problems with care, dissatisfaction, unmet needs or access; and the one included study that observed care, 683 visits to nine psychiatric emergency services in California in 1985–1986, found better care for patients with substance use problems than for other patients on all four criteria, a result the review's text does not mention (van Boekel et al., 2013). The review searched three databases in English and Dutch, excluded studies from Asia, Africa and South America and studies of training, weighted all studies equally whatever their response rate (31% to 92% where given), and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 by the study card; its abstract's statements that negative attitudes reduced patients' empowerment and treatment outcomes rest on two qualitative studies. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Do health workers see and treat people who use drugs differently? In studies from 2000 to 2011, mostly surveys, many health workers said they felt negatively about patients with drug or alcohol problems, or less positive than about patients with other illnesses, more often outside specialist drug and alcohol services; some studies found neutral or positive views. Whether this changes care was studied only a few times, and the results differed: in one study, people who felt treated unfairly by staff were less likely to finish treatment; in another, doctors' views were not linked to what patients said about their care; and the one study that watched real visits, from the 1980s, found better care for these patients.
population: Health professionals (nurses, doctors, staff of drug, alcohol and mental-health services, mixed groups) and, in five papers, their patients, in 28 papers published 2000–2011 from Australia, the UK, the USA, Canada, Ireland and eight European countries
exposure: Being a patient with an alcohol or drug use disorder (the patient group professionals were asked about or treated)
comparator: Patients with other conditions (for example depression, diabetes or other mental illness) where studies compared them; otherwise none
outcome: Professionals' self-reported attitudes, regard and implicit associations; patients' perceived discrimination, treatment completion and reports of care; observed quality of care
magnitude: No pooled estimate and no count of studies by direction. As reported by van Boekel et al. (2013): 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples); regard lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems among 866 professionals in 8 European countries; at least 6 of the study summaries describe moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive attitudes (editors' count of Table 5); 5 papers link more experience or contact with more positive attitudes. Consequences: perceived staff discrimination predicted not completing treatment (92 clients, Sydney); physicians' attitudes not associated with patients' reports of care (2,864 patients with HIV, 373 physicians; 23.2% of the patients had physicians with negative attitudes towards people who inject drugs); better care for patients with substance use problems on all 4 criteria in 683 observed emergency visits (California, 1985–1986).

risk_of_bias.note: A systematic review with critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2 (no protocol; three databases in English and Dutch, PsycINFO giving 10 records; no list of excluded studies; studies weighted equally whatever their design or response rate, from 31% to 92%; conclusions about consequences not tempered by the designs behind them; card sc_van_boekel_2013), whose primary studies are mostly self-reported attitudes from self-selected respondents.

inconsistency.note: Attitude findings and consequence findings both point in different directions; the statement reports both directions and the status is mixed, so the claim is not downgraded twice for the same problem.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the statement describes what professionals reported, in the countries and years covered, and says that care itself was rarely measured.

imprecision.note: Not applicable to a narrative description without pooled estimates.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not judged for a descriptive summary.

grade.reasoning: Observational studies (mostly cross-sectional surveys and qualitative studies) seen through one systematic review: starts low; down one for risk of bias: very low. Rated as worded: the statement describes what the included studies reported, not how common negative attitudes are (the review gives no count), and gives the evidence on care as a handful of studies pointing different ways, including the observational study finding better care that the review leaves out of its text and the null survey result it notes without weighing (card reporting issues). Not used: the abstract's statements that negative attitudes diminished empowerment and treatment outcomes (two qualitative studies), and the recommendation of training (cross-sectional associations, after studies of training were excluded). A causal claim, that health workers' attitudes worsen care, would be insufficient evidence. Status mixed: findings on attitudes and on consequences differ between studies without an explanation the review can settle. The review is systematic, not narrative, so the claim is not narrative-only.

verification.flag_note: Question 10, second part. One review covering 2000–2011, from Western countries only. statement: In people released from prison or jail in eight mostly high-income countries between 1980 and 2018, the death rate was highest in the first week after release, and deaths coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in that week, although most such deaths happened later. In 18 record-linkage cohorts of everyone released (1,471,526 people, 88.3% of them men, in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 75,427 deaths), the pooled crude death rate was 1,612 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 1,048 to 2,287) in days 2 to 7 after release, against 725 (625 to 831) over the whole follow-up and 737 (636 to 844) more than a year after release; the first week's rate was 1.5 times that of the second week (1.2 to 1.8), 2.0 times that of weeks 3–4 (1.5 to 2.6) and 2.2 times that of weeks 9–12 (1.6 to 3.0). The 'first week' starts on day 2 because in some cohorts deaths in custody had been recorded as deaths on the day of release, which inflated the release-day rate (4,036 per 100,000 person-years, falling to 826 in the ten cohorts that could separate the two). Deaths whose underlying cause was coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning, of unintentional or undetermined intent, a single category that does not separate alcohol, other drugs or combinations and names no drug, had a rate of 657 (332 to 1,076) in days 2 to 7, above suicide (135) and heart and blood vessel disease (71), and of 146 (103 to 197) over the whole follow-up, where they were the leading cause (16,126 deaths, 21.4%); yet 14,671 of these 16,126 deaths (91.0%) happened more than 4 weeks after release (Borschmann et al., 2024), since most of the time people were followed lies beyond the first weeks (the editors' explanation). The study compared periods after release with one another, not with the general population; rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1,183 per 100,000 person-years over the whole follow-up) and regions (days 2 to 7: Europe 2,762, the USA 934); causes came from death registers whose certification and coding were not checked across countries and decades; and it recorded nothing about drug use, treatment in custody or tolerance, so it cannot show why deaths cluster soon after release. Whether, and how fast, tolerance falls during a break from opioids is a separate answer, which rests on reviews (see the answer on tolerance after a break from opioids). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Is the time just after leaving prison more dangerous? Yes, most of all the first week. In about 1.5 million people released from prison in eight countries, deaths in days 2 to 7 after release were about 1.5 to 2 times as common as in the weeks that followed. Poisoning by alcohol or other drugs was the most common cause of death, in that first week and overall. Still, 91 in 100 of these poisoning deaths happened more than 4 weeks after release. The records did not say which drugs were involved, and nobody measured drug use or tolerance, so the study cannot say why the first week is riskier.
population: People released from incarceration (prison or jail) in 18 cohorts of everyone released in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA, 1980–2018 (1,471,526 people; 88.3% men)
exposure: Time since release (days 2–7, week 2, weeks 3–4, weeks 9–12, more than a year)
comparator: Later periods after release in the same cohorts (no comparison with the general population)
outcome: Crude death rates per 100,000 person-years, all causes and by underlying cause coded in death registers (alcohol and other drug poisoning of unintentional or undetermined intent; suicide; cardiovascular disease)
magnitude: Borschmann et al. (2024), pooled crude rates per 100,000 person-years: all causes, days 2–7 1612 (95% CI 1048–2287), I² 91.1%; whole follow-up 725 (625–831); more than 1 year 737 (636–844); first week vs week 2 IRR 1.5 (1.2–1.8), vs weeks 3–4 2.0 (1.5–2.6), vs weeks 9–12 2.2 (1.6–3.0). Days 2–7 by cause: alcohol and other drug poisoning 657 (332–1076), suicide 135 (36–277), cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). Whole follow-up: poisoning 146 (103–197), 16,126 of 75,427 deaths (21.4%); 14,671 of the 16,126 (91.0%) more than 4 weeks after release. Release day 4036 (887–8940), 826 (0–3455) in the ten cohorts that separated deaths in custody. Cohorts 236 to 1183; days 2–7 Europe 2762 (1832–3872), USA 934 (389–1703). Excluding time back in custody (16 cohorts) 720 (605–845).

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the all-cause first-week pattern: complete release cohorts linked to death registers and analysed under one plan, with sensitivity analyses for deaths in custody recorded on the day of release and for time back in custody (720 against 725). The cause-specific figures are less certain: death certification, toxicology and the coding of drug deaths and of undetermined intent were not appraised across eight countries and four decades (card sc_borschmann_2024: AMSTAR 2 critically low), and three Western Australian cohorts overlap in place and time.

inconsistency.note: I² is 91% for days 2–7 and 99–100% over the whole follow-up, and cohort rates range from 236 to 1,183, but the first-week excess holds in the pooled rate ratios with moderate heterogeneity (I² 26% against week 2); the heterogeneity concerns the size of the rates, which the statement gives with their range.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded for these mostly high-income cohorts, mostly men; the statement says that the poisoning category names no drug and includes alcohol and deaths of undetermined intent.

imprecision.note: The days 2–7 intervals are wide (all causes 1,048 to 2,287; poisoning 332 to 1,076), but the rate ratios against later periods exclude 1 (1.5, 1.2 to 1.8).

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the study; an individual participant data consortium analysed under one plan is less exposed to selective publication.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive (crude death rates by time since release): starts low; not downgraded and not upgraded (descriptive claims are never upgraded). The rating applies to the all-cause pattern; the poisoning figures, taken alone, would be rated very low for risk of bias (unappraised cause-of-death coding across countries and decades), and the statement labels them as coded causes that name no drug. Status single study: one individual participant data meta-analysis; the cohort-by-cohort results by time since release are in the appendix, which was not read, so the 18 cohorts are not counted as independent replications here, and earlier studies of deaths after release (for example Binswanger et al., 2007, whose Washington cohort is one of the 18) were not read. The first-week peak and the 91.0% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks hold together because most person-time lies beyond the first weeks (study card note; the editors' explanation in the statement). Nothing about tolerance was measured, and the claim does not attribute the early peak to it.
